Expert 1
Senior Director, IT Infrastructure and Operations at Pharma Company (2025 - present)
Interview Introduction
Hello!
Hello, I'm the Synquery interviewer. Could you please tell me your name and confirm you're ready to start?
Yes, Travis, and I'm ready to start.

Hi Travis, I'm Q, an AI interviewer from Synquery. I'm looking forward to our conversation today. Just a heads up: there might be some unnatural pauses, and I might accidentally interrupt you. If I do, please feel free to talk over me to finish your thought. Does that sound okay?
Yes.
Great. To start, could you please give me a brief background of your experience related to enterprise ITSM platform evaluation?

Yeah, sure. I currently serve as the Senior Director of IT Infrastructure and Operations. I oversee all aspects of IT—infrastructure, applications, security—pretty much everything related to IT. I'm the head of IT for my current company, Xena, and I oversee ITSM. Currently we have a custom ITSM; previously we used ServiceNow.
Current ServiceNow Environment

Thanks for sharing that, Travis—that's helpful. Let's start with your time at your previous employer where you used ServiceNow. Can you walk me through how that organization used the platform and which specific modules you deployed?

Yeah, I used ServiceNow at my previous stop, Thermo Fisher. It was a very large implementation—about a $40B company with roughly 2,000 sites. We handled around 2M tickets annually. The modules we used included Incident, Request, Problem, Change, and Knowledge. We had a full Configuration Management Database (CMDB), Asset Management, and Major Incident Management. We also used HR—many HR service requests ran through ServiceNow. And we started implementing GRC as another module.
That's a very extensive deployment. What were the key drivers that led Thermo Fisher to adopt ServiceNow in the first place?

The key drivers were faster resolution of IT tickets and reducing MTTR. We were on, I believe, Zendesk at the time, and needed better, faster performance and improved routing. We also needed centralized management of all IT assets. So, multiple drivers, but really it was about improving service levels (SLAs), MTTR, and the user experience from an IT perspective.

You mentioned improving service levels and user experience. Were those goals part of a broader strategic initiative, like a digital transformation or an effort to consolidate fragmented IT tools across the organization?
Can you repeat the question?

Of course. I was asking if the goals of improving service levels and user experience were part of a larger company initiative, such as a digital transformation program or an effort to bring different IT tools together onto one platform.

Yes, it was about consolidating a lot of the IT tools—some of it was even paper-based. We wanted to improve service levels and MTTR and also be able to track our assets. In addition, we wanted better compliance—we’re subject to heavy regulations such as SOC, ISO, GxP, and SOC 2. ServiceNow can help with controls around our IT assets and equipment, so that was another driver.

You’ve already mentioned expanding into asset management and HR Service Delivery. What were the specific business needs that drove you to adopt those modules? You also mentioned implementing GRSD. Could you clarify which module that was?

The module was GRC—Governance, Risk, and Compliance. Basically, you can load all of your risks. For example, if you haven’t done a pen test on a server in a while, that’s a risk because the system hasn’t been stress-tested for security. That would be logged in the GRC module as a risk, then categorized and prioritized. And could you repeat the other part of your question?
Thanks for clarifying GRC. My other question was about the drivers for expanding into asset management and HR Service Delivery. What specific business needs led to those decisions?

For asset management, we needed better inventory of our assets to support lifecycle management. For HR, they were handling a lot of tickets via phone, paper, and email, so we needed a consolidated system to improve service delivery and tracking from an HR perspective. Those were two big drivers.

That makes sense. Was the decision to expand into modules like asset management, HR, and GRC driven more by a top-down, enterprise-wide strategy, or did it come from specific departments identifying pain points and requesting a solution?

The pain points really started at the site and division levels, and then it became a strategic digital transformation initiative. There were a lot of complaints about slowness—in both the process and service levels—which weren’t great. This was observed at the lower levels, typically at the site level, the manufacturing plants. They have a site lead and an IT partner. From there, you go up to the divisions, where you have a division lead. Once we started seeing commonality across sites and divisions, it moved up to a strategic initiative from an IT global perspective. So, it started at the site level, grew into a strategic IT initiative, and then was implemented globally.

I’d like to follow up on a few things you’ve mentioned. That’s a very clear explanation of bottom-up demand driving a top-down strategic decision. First, you said you’re currently using a custom ITSM at Abzena, which is a big shift from the large-scale ServiceNow environment at Thermo Fisher. What makes a custom solution the right fit for Abzena today instead of a commercial platform?

Great question. I’ve been with Abzena for about 6 months, and that decision was made by my predecessor. We actually had ServiceNow at one point, but they felt that for the size of the company it was too complicated for end users. They also wanted to take advantage of AI, so this custom solution integrates with Microsoft Teams—you can talk to it, and it can create a ticket. It has AI capabilities to recognize an IT issue, try some troubleshooting, and if it can’t resolve it, it creates a ticket. At that time, ServiceNow’s agents weren’t as advanced, and this was more simplified. The backend is also easier to manage. Personally, I’m not sure why they made the move—I think it was poorly implemented and then they decided to switch. Not my decision; it predated me and we have to live with it. One repercussion is we don’t really have asset management for all our IT assets, which is a big pain point for me right now. We’re now looking at possibly implementing just the ServiceNow asset management piece to categorize all our GMP equipment and IT assets. I don’t think the decision was well thought through and it doesn’t scale, but for the company size at that time, I guess it made sense to simplify the user experience.

That’s a fascinating situation, dealing with the consequences of a predecessor’s decision. It sounds like you’re trying to find a hybrid approach to fill the gaps. Let’s go back to Thermo Fisher for a moment. You mentioned that GxP and SOX compliance were major drivers for adopting ServiceNow over tools like Zendesk. What specific capabilities did ServiceNow have for compliance that Zendesk lacked? Was it about having better audit trails, or were there specific workflow controls that were essential?
Could you repeat the question?
Certainly. What specific compliance features did ServiceNow offer for GxP and SOX that your previous tool, Zendesk, was missing?

Yes. Number one, the system was validated. For example, when you enter a change, you can check a box indicating it’s GxP-related. If it’s GxP-related, it triggers specific workflows for routing and the change process that Zendesk did not have. It provided more robust functionality for a typical GxP-related change. Typically, you have an IT change that then goes to Quality; Quality opens a change, it gets approved and reviewed, you might have to do testing, etc. ServiceNow offered more customization and out-of-the-box functionality than Zendesk, including advanced routing and workflows to accommodate GxP processes.
Vendor Selection & Decision Criteria

That makes a lot of sense. The ability to enforce validated workflows for regulated changes is a clear differentiator. Now, let’s shift to the vendor selection process. When you were evaluating ITSM platforms at Thermo Fisher, what alternatives to ServiceNow were you aware of and actively considering?

We looked at competitors like Jira. We also considered that Workday had some ticket management capabilities. We looked at Zendesk again. We actually looked at quite a few different systems. The biggest ones were Jira, BMC’s tool, and a few others I’m blanking on.
That’s a good list.
Yeah.
BMC and Zendesk. When you were making that selection, what were your top 3-5 purchasing criteria?
The first thing is functionality.
Okay, functionality is number one. What else?

Functionality. Next was user experience. Then how the system scales—can it support growth within 3-5 years? We also looked at integration—can it integrate with our identity and access management (IAM), with Workday (our HR/HCM system)? We also considered automation—what can it do in terms of automatic routing, etc. There was reporting and analytics, total cost of ownership, and some softer considerations like vendor reputation.
That's a comprehensive list.
Functionality.
Functionality, user experience, scalability, integration, automation, reporting, TCO, and vendor reputation. Could you rank the top 3-5 of those in strict priority order for me?
Yes. Give me a minute—I'm thinking.
Of course, take your time.

I’d say the first is integration capabilities. At that scale, it has to work with your other systems. The second is scalability. Third would be cost, or total cost of ownership. Fourth, the user experience. And fifth, customization.

Great—so your top five are: 1) integration, 2) scalability, 3) cost/TCO, 4) user experience, and 5) customization. Focusing on your top criterion—integration capabilities—what specific evidence or demonstrations from a vendor would have proven they met your requirements? For example, were you looking for reference architectures, a proof of concept, or customer references?

First, we’d want a live demo of the capabilities. From there, we might ask for customer references, but we’d start with a product demonstration to show they truly have the capabilities. Next, a short POC to prove it. For example, on integration, we’d ask, can you integrate with Workday? If they said yes in the demo, we’d say, show us. In their environment, they’d run a small POC: here’s ServiceNow integrated with Workday—when a new employee is onboarded, it flows right into the ServiceNow process.

That’s very clear—so a live demo followed by a targeted proof of concept was key for validating those integration claims. With that in mind, what ultimately tipped the decision in ServiceNow’s favor over alternatives like Jira and BMC?
They had strong integration and strong scalability. They weren’t as strong on cost—they were a bit higher—but integration, scalability, and customization tipped the scale.
So even though cost was higher, the strength in integration, scalability, and customization outweighed it. Was there one single factor?
Go ahead.
Was it the integration, the scalability, or the customization that truly set ServiceNow apart from the rest?

I’d say scalability. We were at a point where the volume of data and manual workflows in our previous system wasn’t scalable. When we left it, we were at around 2M tickets per year, and trying to do that on the previous system would just break it. So scalability was the top criterion—working with a Fortune 500 company at roughly $40B revenue and 2,000 sites—this was critical.

That makes perfect sense. At that scale, the ability to handle the sheer volume of transactions without breaking is non-negotiable. You mentioned integration and scalability were your top two priorities—where did alternatives like Jira and BMC fall short? For example, did Jira struggle with handling 2M tickets, or did BMC lack the necessary connectors for your ecosystem?

At the time, Jira wasn’t scalable enough and lacked modules we needed. We were concerned that at 1-2M tickets we’d hit performance issues. Jira is great for agile software project management, but we worried about handling infrastructure issues, major incident management, and change management. Zendesk is very intuitive for customer service and fits small to mid-market needs, but it lacks advanced workflow automation and customization. We were already seeing performance issues as our data volume grew.

That’s a very clear breakdown of the limitations you saw in Jira and Zendesk. Now, regarding cost, you noted that ServiceNow was the more expensive choice. Can you give me a rough idea of how significant that price difference was? Was it a 20-30% [AUDIO UNKNOWN]?

If we set ServiceNow at about $100 per user/month as a baseline, I’d put Zendesk at roughly $50-55. Jira was very inexpensive but lacked capabilities—around $20-21. So compared to Zendesk, ServiceNow was almost double.
With ServiceNow being nearly double the cost of Zendesk, what specific argument convinced your finance department to approve that significantly higher investment?

The business case focused on scalability. We were growing—from roughly a $20B company to about $30B—and adding around 10-50K users. We were already seeing performance issues, and ticket management wasn’t meeting GMP/GxP requirements. That case was presented to finance mainly to confirm budget alignment, but the real decision-makers were senior IT leadership. Directors and senior directors typically drive the business case; a global IT senior director/director helps assemble it. Approval then goes to the VP level. Depending on the spend, the CIO may also sign off, but that’s primarily to confirm budget and due diligence. Most of the influence and decision-making happens at the director, senior director, and VP levels.

Great breakdown of the internal approval process. It sounds like the business case—grounded in scalability and compliance—justified the premium for the key decision makers at the director and VP levels. Now, moving to a direct competitive comparison: thinking back to your key purchasing criteria, how did ServiceNow perform against each of them compared to competitors like BMC and Jira? Let’s start with your number one criterion: integration capabilities.
For integration, I’d rate ServiceNow 9/10. Zendesk 6/10. Jira 7/10. BMC 7/10.
Okay.
Scalability: ServiceNow about 9.5/10, very scalable. BMC around 8/10. Jira about 5/10. Zendesk about 5/10.
Got it. And for total cost of ownership?

Total cost of ownership would come down to this: ServiceNow is very expensive—I'd put it at a 6. Jira is very economical—I'd give it a 9. Zendesk is probably a 7. And BMC is also very expensive—maybe a 7.
How about user experience?

Yeah, good question. For user experience, I would say Jira has a really strong user experience; I'd give it an 8 out of 10. Zendesk is very simple—it's a pretty simplified and easy-to-use experience, and so is the backend—so I'd give it an 8. ServiceNow can have its complexity depending on how you configure it, so I'd give it a 7. And then BMC is probably a little bit easier to use; I'd give it an 8.
And finally, customization.

Yeah, good question. ServiceNow: a 9—you can customize pretty much everything with ServiceNow. Jira has some customization; I'd probably put it at a 6. Zendesk: a 6 as well. BMC offers more customization—maybe an 8.
Competitive Comparison

Thanks for those ratings. That's a really helpful breakdown. Based on that, where do you see the gap between ServiceNow and its competitors being the smallest? In other words, which of your criteria is the one where a competitor like Atlassian or BMC comes closest to matching or even outperforming ServiceNow?
Probably BMC comes closest.
And on which criterion does BMC come closest? Is it on user experience, cost, or something else?
Customization, scalability, and integration.

Interesting. So you feel BMC is quite close on your top criteria. Other experts I've spoken with have often highlighted ServiceNow's main vulnerabilities as its high cost and implementation complexity. They suggest [AUDIO UNKNOWN] and Freshservice often win deals by promising significantly lower total cost of ownership and faster deployment times. However, enterprises still choose ServiceNow when they need comprehensive ITIL process coverage and deep integration capabilities. Does that align with your experience?
Yes, agreed.

You've operated ServiceNow at massive scale. Looking back, how would you compare its overall capabilities to the alternatives you've seen or evaluated? Do you feel its breadth is truly unmatched, even if competitors excel in specific niches?

I'm very impressed with their CEO. He's significantly grown the company's market cap [AUDIO UNKNOWN] and has a strong vision. They had some poor leadership in the past, and he's really turned the company around. I admire that they're leaning headfirst into AI—now they have agents, and with the Moveworks acquisition as well. They're driving a major digital transformation from what was just an ITIL system into HR and broader service management, and now they want to get into the CRM space. I think they're well-positioned to compete against Salesforce. Overall, the functionality and scalability are very strong.

It sounds like you see their strategic direction and expansion beyond core ITSM as a major strength. How does ServiceNow stack up against competitors specifically when it comes to ease of use and day-to-day operational complexity for your team?

We have dedicated admins who maintain it, customize it, and create new flows, so there is ongoing work. You can also engage partners to help. There’s definitely maintenance and upkeep—probably more than other competitors because it can be a very complex system. You need dedicated admins, and partners for more advanced configurations and integrations.
Given that complexity, are there any specific areas where you feel competitors have a distinct advantage over ServiceNow?

It's a good question. I'd point to BMC as one example. Obviously, cost is number one—many competitors are lower cost. But they typically don't have as much capability and flexibility as ServiceNow. Jira is making a run at AI, which makes it quite competitive. And Zendesk is simple—they keep the user experience simple, which makes it easier for users and simpler to maintain with straightforward workflows. That's an advantage.
So, to summarize, you see competitors having advantages in three main areas: lower cost, simplicity of user experience, and—in Jira's case—a growing focus on AI. Is that right?
Yeah, well said.

I'd like to follow up on a couple of things from this section. You mentioned that your current company, Xena, moved away from ServiceNow partly because its AI capabilities were lacking at the time. Yet, you just praised ServiceNow's current AI strategy as a major strength. Do you think their recent acquisitions, like Moveworks, have closed that gap enough to prevent a mid-sized company from making a similar switch today?

At the time, they weren’t leaning into it as heavily; the vendor we chose was taking an AI-first approach. That was the major difference. Since then, I think they’ve grown in their AI capabilities. Cost was also a factor—we saw lower licensing costs.

That makes sense. It was a matter of timing and cost. You also noted that ServiceNow requires dedicated admins and partners to manage its complexity. At the scale of Thermo Fisher, what was the actual headcount required to maintain the platform? Was it a small team of 3-5 people, or a much larger department? And did that ongoing labor cost ever challenge the ROI of the platform?

It was about 3-5 employees, each allocated around 30-40% of their time to maintain the system. For more complex needs—major upgrades or complex flows—we engaged partners. Did that impact ROI? Slightly, but we were able to scale to the point where it still made sense.
Implementation & Integration

That’s a very efficient team for such a large deployment. It sounds like you used a blended model of internal staff for day-to-day work and partners for heavy lifting, which helped protect the overall ROI. Let’s move on to the implementation itself. What was your implementation experience like at Thermo Fisher, and what were the biggest challenges you faced?

Great question. The implementation was quite complex and took roughly 9-12 months to fully complete. The biggest pain points were lacking a clear definition of done—there was so much customization that scope boundaries were fuzzy—and underestimating the internal effort required. User testing wasn’t clearly defined, so we had to pull in resources who weren’t expecting it, and it was hard to secure their time.

So, a 9-12 month timeline. The key challenges were a lack of a clear vision for done and underestimating the internal resource commitment needed for things like user acceptance testing. How well did ServiceNow integrate with your other major enterprise systems, like Microsoft Azure, SAP, and your various security tools?

It integrated well, but it took time to build. We set up single sign-on with Active Directory and integrated Workday. Let's move to cost. How did Freshservice's total cost of ownership compare to what you initially budgeted?
Pretty close to budget, honestly - maybe 5% over, mostly because we added a few more agent seats than planned once field supervisors wanted access.
Can you give a rough sense of per-agent pricing, or how it compared to the alternatives you evaluated?

We're on a tier that comes out to roughly forty dollars per agent per month. ServiceNow's quote for a comparable scope was north of one-fifty. Ivanti was around fifty-five. Zendesk for IT was close to us, maybe thirty-five.
Were there any licensing surprises?

The Project module was an add-on we hadn't originally budgeted for - that came later once we decided we wanted it for infrastructure rollouts. Otherwise, pretty transparent pricing overall, which I appreciated.
How has renewal pricing trended?
We're two renewals in, increases have been around 6 to 8 percent each time, which is a bit more than I'd like, but manageable.
Platform Satisfaction & Loyalty
On a scale of 1 to 10, how likely are you to continue using Freshservice over the next three years?
I'd say an 8.
And on a 0 to 10 scale, how likely would you recommend Freshservice to a peer at a similarly sized company?
A 9. For our size and use case, it's been a really good fit.
What do you see as Freshservice's biggest strengths?
Ease of use, fast implementation, solid asset management for the price, and genuinely good customer support when we've had issues.
And its biggest weaknesses?

The automation builder getting clunky at complexity, renewal price creep, and I'd say reporting could be more flexible - we've had to export to Excel more than I'd like for certain board-level reports.
Can you give a specific example of when one of those weaknesses caused a real business impact?

The reporting limitation, mainly. When our CFO's office wanted a specific SOC 2 audit trail report in a particular format, we ended up building it manually in Excel every quarter rather than pulling it natively, which is just wasted time.
Was that a platform limitation, or something that better configuration could solve?

A bit of both - Freshservice's native reporting is decent for standard use cases, but for a very specific custom compliance format, it just doesn't flex enough without going into their analytics add-on, which we haven't purchased.
Switching Dynamics
How difficult would it be for Solara to migrate away from Freshservice if leadership decided to?
I'd put it around a 4 out of 10. We're not deeply entangled - the integrations are fairly standard, and our data model isn't overly customized. It'd be a project, but not a nightmare.
What would trigger you to seriously evaluate switching?

If we scaled significantly, say tripled in size, I'd want to re-evaluate whether Freshservice's automation and reporting could keep up, or whether something like ServiceNow would finally make sense. Also a serious support quality drop would do it.
If you were to switch, which alternative would you look at first?
Probably ServiceNow, just because if we're big enough to justify switching costs, I'd want the platform with the most long-term headroom.
Interview Wrap-up
That's all the questions I have for today, Marcus. This has been a really insightful conversation about Freshservice in a mid-market renewable energy environment. Thank you for your time.
No problem, glad to help.
Is there anything else you'd like to add before we wrap up?
No, I think that covers it well.
Great. Well, Marcus, thank you so much for your time and for sharing your expertise today. I'll be ending the call now.
Thanks, take care.
